title: Sampling, bias, confidence intervals, precision

sections.title: How to use this toolkit
sections.html:
Work through Sections 1–5 in order. Section 1 defines whom the analysis represents. Section 2 asks whether the observed customers can represent them. Sections 3–5 turn the sample into estimates and decision-relevant intervals. Recalculate each result before using the Excel 365 or SPSS route. The Try it questions are ungraded checks; their answers appear immediately below them.

The core crosswalk is sampling terminology and methods, sampling distributions, estimation, confidence intervals for one mean and one proportion, and sample-size logic (H001–H008, H011–H017). Bias and independence (H018–H021) are necessary limits on those calculations. Intervals for differences between groups (H009–H010) receive a short optional bridge in Section 5; comparison and testing are developed in later sessions.

This course has no required textbook. The supplied Albright and Winston and Field headings are scope cues, not chapters you are claimed to have read. This original synthesis is grounded in the open university teaching materials and official software documentation actually cited below. This Markdown source has no stable PDF page numbers. Future slides and PNP materials should cite its stable numbered section headings; page references can be added only after pagination.

sections.title: Fictional running case: Cedar Loop grocery pickup
sections.html:
Cedar Loop is entirely fictional. Its pickup manager must decide whether to add a staff member during the evening handoff period. The stakeholder is the pickup manager; the decision is whether to pilot extra staffing, not whether the current sample “proves” staffing will work. The proposed KPI is the share of pickups taking more than 50 minutes from order-ready notification to handoff, with a managerial target of at most 20%. A guardrail is that any pilot must not increase labor cost per pickup beyond a separately approved budget. The descriptive claim to investigate is that the population’s slow-pickup share may exceed 20%.

Case elementDefinition or fictional evidence
Population and periodAll 2,400 eligible Cedar Loop pickups completed during a specified four-week period
Unit and grainOne completed pickup; one record per unique pickup ID
Sampling frameThe operational list of those 2,400 IDs, if complete and deduplicated
Variablesminutes: notification-to-handoff minutes; slow: 1 if minutes > 50, otherwise 0; period: morning or evening
Proposed selectionSelect 125 distinct IDs uniformly without replacement; invite those customers to confirm their recorded handoff information
Observed responses100 usable pickups; 25 selected pickups lack usable confirmation
Verified sample summariesOf 100 responses, 24 are slow; mean duration xˉ=42\bar x=42 minutes; sample standard deviation s=12s=12 minutes
Decision evidence still missingSlow status of the 25 nonrespondents; frame audit; evening-specific precision; staffing cost and pilot effect

The aggregates are stipulated fictional inputs, not an attached row-level dataset. They let you check arithmetic, but no one can reproduce a row-level output or audit missing values from this chapter alone. Nor does this observational snapshot estimate what adding staff would cause. Keep four statements separate: observation—24 of 100 respondents were slow; assumption—respondents adequately represent the stated population; inference—a population interval conditional on that assumption; recommendation—what evidence to collect before changing staffing.

sections.title: 1. Define the population before drawing conclusions
1.1 Population, frame, sample, and estimate
sections.html:
A population is the full set of units the question concerns: here, 2,400 eligible pickups in the four-week period. A parameter is a fixed but usually unknown population quantity, such as the share pp of those pickups that were slow. A sample is the selected subset. Its statistic, p^\hat p, estimates pp; different selections can produce different p^\hat p values. The sampling frame is the list from which IDs can actually be selected. Check that canceled orders are excluded and that an ID cannot occur twice. These choices precede calculation because “all future customers” is a broader population than this four-week list. (The Pennsylvania State University, n.d.-a, n.d.-b).

A simple random sample of 125 IDs without replacement gives every set of 125 distinct IDs from the frame the same chance of selection. Assign each unique eligible ID a random ordering, retain the first 125, and freeze the selected-ID list before contacting customers. Uniform selection requires a complete frame and an unbiased random procedure; sorting IDs by time and taking the first 125 would not do it. Sampling without replacement also means that two rows with the same pickup ID do not become two independent pickups. (The Pennsylvania State University, n.d.-a).

Worked example. The analysis has 100 usable responses, including 24 slow pickups. Its respondent estimate is

p^=slow usable pickupsusable pickups=24100=0.24=24%.\hat p=\frac{\text{slow usable pickups}}{\text{usable pickups}} =\frac{24}{100}=0.24=24\%.

The numerator and denominator count pickups, not minutes or customers making multiple orders. The 20% target corresponds to 0.20(100)=200.20(100)=20 slow pickups in a group of 100; the observed 24 exceed that comparison by 4 pickups, or 4 percentage points. This is a descriptive observation about respondents. It is not yet evidence that precisely 24% of all 2,400 pickups were slow.

Failure mode: Calling the 100 respondents “a random sample of the population” skips the 25 missing confirmations. Random selection of invitations does not guarantee random response.

Try it — ungraded. If 30 of 120 usable pickups were slow, what is the respondent estimate, and what is its unit?

Answer. Divide like units: 30 pickups/120 pickups=0.2530\text{ pickups}/120\text{ pickups}=0.25, or 25% of usable pickups. It is not “0.25 minutes” and, without a response assessment, not automatically 25% of the population.

sections.title: 1.2 Choose a sampling design and record the draw
sections.html:
Random selection is a property of how IDs enter the sample, not a label added after data arrive. Four common probability designs make different trade-offs (The Pennsylvania State University, n.d.-a, n.d.-e):

DesignCedar Loop procedureBenefitCaution
Simple randomDraw 125 distinct IDs from all 2,400 eligible pickupsEach set of 125 has the same selection chanceA small subgroup may appear sparsely by chance
StratifiedSplit the frame into morning and evening pickups, then draw independently within eachAssures representation of both periodsCombine results with population shares, especially if allocation is disproportionate
ClusterRandomly choose pickup waves and inspect all pickups in those wavesMay reduce collection travel and setupPickups in one wave may be alike, reducing effective information
SystematicChoose a random start from 1–20, then every 20th ID on an ordered listEasy operational selection; yields 120 of 2,400A list cycle aligned with 20 can distort the sample; this example has 120 rather than 125 IDs

Worked example: proportional strata. Suppose the audited frame has 1,440 morning pickups and 960 evening pickups. Their shares are 1,440/2,400=0.601,440/2,400=0.60 and 960/2,400=0.40960/2,400=0.40. For 125 invitations, draw 0.60(125)=750.60(125)=75 morning IDs and 0.40(125)=500.40(125)=50 evening IDs. Then select randomly within each stratum. This protects evening representation without pretending that the 100 eventual responses are automatically representative. If response differs by period, report that and use a defensible design or response adjustment before generalizing.

Reproducible Excel 365 selection. Keep the untouched, deduplicated frame of 2,400 unique IDs. Add =RAND() beside each ID, calculate once, and paste that random column as values before sorting it ascending with ID as a tie-breaker. Save the frozen random values, the selected first 125 IDs, frame date, inclusion rule, and draw date. Reopening the saved file can reproduce which IDs were selected; RAND() alone will recalculate and cannot reproduce the same draw. Verify there are exactly 125 distinct selected IDs and that each appears in the original frame. This selection record is separate from later response and measurement checks.

Try it — ungraded. If Cedar Loop took the first 125 pickup records from Monday morning, which design above would that be, and could a confidence interval alone remove the resulting coverage problem?

Answer. It is a convenience selection, not one of the four probability designs. It misses other times by construction. A narrow interval around those 125 observations describes sampling variation under assumptions it does not satisfy; it cannot repair the omitted periods.

sections.title: 2.1 Selection, missing responses, and the unit of independence
sections.html:
Sampling variability is the difference between estimates obtained from properly selected samples by chance. Bias is a systematic tendency for a selection or measurement process to favor certain results. At Cedar Loop, busy customers whose pickups took longest might be less likely to confirm their records; if so, respondent-only estimates could understate slow pickups. Increasing the number of similarly selected respondents would reduce some random variability but would not repair that mechanism. Nonresponse and measurement errors are distinct from ordinary sampling error. (The Pennsylvania State University, n.d.-a, n.d.-e, n.d.-f).

Independence concerns whether observations provide substantially separate information. One pickup per unique ID avoids literal duplicate records. But pickups by the same customer, or many pickups during a shared outage, might still have related durations. A simple interval that treats those records as independent can be too narrow. Check repeated customer IDs and service incidents using authorized, privacy-protected data; do not export names into a student workbook.

Worked example. Of Cedar Loop’s 125 selected pickups, 100 have usable confirmations, so the usable-response rate is 100/125=0.80=80%100/125=0.80=80\%. The respondent slow share is 24/100=24%24/100=24\%. To see why response matters, hold the observed 24 slow pickups fixed and make two sensitivity assumptions about the 25 missing ones:

  • If none was slow, the share among the 125 selected pickups would be (24+0)/125=19.2%(24+0)/125=19.2\%.
  • If all 25 were slow, it would be (24+25)/125=39.2%(24+25)/125=39.2\%.

These are bounds for the selected set under extreme missing-outcome scenarios, not a confidence interval for all 2,400 pickups. Their spread crosses the 20% target. It shows why response follow-up can be more useful than another decimal place in an interval. An operational next step is to compare respondents with nonrespondents on permitted frame information, check timestamps against source records, and follow up selected nonrespondents through an approved process. Such checks can reveal concerns; matching observed fields alone cannot prove that missing outcomes are harmless. (The Pennsylvania State University, n.d.-f).

[KEY] Precision is not representativeness. A narrow interval based on a biased respondent group can be confidently wrong about the intended population.

Failure mode: Treating the extreme 19.2%–39.2% range as a “95% interval.” It has no 95% coverage calculation; it changes an assumption about missing values instead.

Try it — ungraded. Suppose follow-up verifies that 10 of the 25 missing Cedar Loop pickups were slow. What would the slow share be among all 125 selected pickups? Does this alone reveal the exact share among all 2,400?

Answer. (24+10)/125=34/125=0.272=27.2%(24+10)/125=34/125=0.272=27.2\%. The selected set is now more complete. Its result still varies from what another properly selected set might produce, so it is not the exact population parameter.

sections.title: 3. Understand standard error before an interval
3.1 From variation in pickups to variation in estimates
sections.html:
The crosswalk's SPINE cue links Standard error, Parameters, Intervals, Null-hypothesis testing, and Estimation. For this session, name the population parameter first, use a sample to estimate it, calculate the standard error under an appropriate design, then construct and interpret an interval. Formal null-hypothesis testing is developed in the next teaching unit; the mnemonic is a navigation aid, not a formula or a claim that all five steps occur in every analysis.

The standard deviation ss describes variation among observed pickup durations: Cedar Loop’s s=12s=12 minutes. The standard error (SE) describes variation in a statistic across repeated samples of the same design. For an approximately independent simple random sample, estimate the mean’s SE by s/ns/\sqrt n. The distribution of means that repeated samples would produce is the sampling distribution. With a sufficiently large, appropriate sample, the central limit theorem helps make that distribution approximately normal even when individual durations are not normal. It does not remove selection bias or make dependent records independent. (The Pennsylvania State University, n.d.-b, n.d.-c).

Worked example. Using Cedar Loop’s 100 usable durations as an illustrative independent sample:

SExˉ=sn=12 minutes100=1210=1.20 minutes.SE_{\bar x}=\frac{s}{\sqrt n} =\frac{12\text{ minutes}}{\sqrt{100}} =\frac{12}{10} =1.20\text{ minutes}.

That is not a claim that most individual pickups lie within 1.20 minutes of the mean. It describes how a sample mean would vary under repeated comparable sampling. If the usable sample instead contained 400 independent pickups with similar s=12s=12, its estimated SE would be 12/400=0.6012/\sqrt{400}=0.60 minute: four times the usable sample size gives half the SE. That calculation assumes the additional observations remain appropriate and that their variability stays similar. Cedar Loop cannot obtain 400 independent confirmations merely by copying its 100 rows four times. (The Pennsylvania State University, n.d.-b).

For a binary slow indicator, an illustrative SE is

SEp^=p^(1−p^)n=0.24(0.76)100=0.001824≈0.04271,SE_{\hat p} =\sqrt{\frac{\hat p(1-\hat p)}{n}} =\sqrt{\frac{0.24(0.76)}{100}} =\sqrt{0.001824} \approx0.04271,

or about 4.27 percentage points. This is variability of the estimated share, not a 4.27% chance that any particular pickup is slow. The usual formulas also assume the relevant sample behaves approximately like independent random observations; Section 2 explains why Cedar Loop must audit that premise. (The Pennsylvania State University, n.d.-c).

Failure mode: Dividing the standard deviation by nn, rather than n\sqrt n, would give 12/100=0.1212/100=0.12 minute and falsely suggest far greater precision.

Try it — ungraded. A comparable sample has n=144n=144 independent pickups and s=18s=18 minutes. Find the estimated SE of its mean.

Answer. 144=12\sqrt{144}=12, so SExˉ=18/12=1.5SE_{\bar x}=18/12=1.5 minutes. Keep the minutes: the statistic is a mean duration.

sections.title: 4. Estimate a population mean with a confidence interval
4.1 The mean, margin of error, and 95% procedure
sections.html:
A confidence interval combines a point estimate and a margin of error, the distance from its center to either endpoint. For a population mean with unknown population standard deviation, the familiar one-sample tt interval is

xˉ ± t∗sn,\bar x\ \pm\ t^*\frac{s}{\sqrt n},

where t∗t^* is the two-sided critical value with n−1n-1 degrees of freedom. Use it when the selection and independence conditions are credible and the distribution of the sample mean is adequately approximated. Inspect the data for extreme duration errors; a large nn is not permission to retain impossible timestamps. A 95% procedure is designed so that, under its assumptions, about 95% of intervals produced across repeated samples cover the fixed population mean. It does not assign a 95% probability to this particular fixed mean lying in this already calculated interval. (The Pennsylvania State University, n.d.-b, n.d.-c).

Worked example. For the 100 usable Cedar Loop durations, xˉ=42\bar x=42 minutes, s=12s=12 minutes, and SExˉ=1.20SE_{\bar x}=1.20 minutes. There are 100−1=99100-1=99 degrees of freedom. The two-sided 95% critical value is approximately t∗=1.9842t^*=1.9842. Calculate each endpoint:

M=1.9842(1.20)=2.3810 minutes;42−2.3810=39.6190;42+2.3810=44.3810.M=1.9842(1.20)=2.3810\text{ minutes}; \qquad 42-2.3810=39.6190; \qquad 42+2.3810=44.3810.

Rounded to reporting precision, the illustrative 95% interval is 39.62 to 44.38 minutes. Conditional on a defensible sampling and response process, it estimates the mean duration of eligible pickups in the stated period. It does not say that 95% of individual pickups lasted between those endpoints. Because Cedar Loop has unresolved nonresponse, report the interval alongside that limitation rather than presenting it as fully validated population coverage. (The Pennsylvania State University, n.d.-c).

Excel 365, after the calculation. If an audited sheet has one numeric duration per usable pickup in B2:B101, first check that =COUNT(B2:B101) returns 100, =AVERAGE(B2:B101) returns 42, and =STDEV.S(B2:B101) returns 12. If it does not, investigate rows or rounding rather than forcing the result. For this exercise’s stipulated summaries, place 100, 42, and 12 in E2:E4. Then use =E4/SQRT(E2) for the SE, =T.INV.2T(0.05,E2-1) for t∗t^*, and =E3-T.INV.2T(0.05,E2-1)*E4/SQRT(E2) and the corresponding + formula for endpoints. STDEV.S estimates a sample standard deviation; Microsoft documents the statistical functions used here. A summary-only sheet checks arithmetic but cannot validate the missing row-level data. (Microsoft, n.d.).

SPSS, when an authorized row-level file exists. Verify that it has one usable row per pickup, numeric minutes, and the same missing-value rule. Run EXAMINE VARIABLES=minutes /STATISTICS=DESCRIPTIVES /CINTERVAL 95. and compare its valid nn, mean, standard deviation, and 95% CI for Mean with the hand calculation. Do not claim the stipulated aggregates are reproducible in SPSS without those rows. IBM documents EXAMINE’s descriptive output and its confidence-level option. (IBM, n.d.-a, n.d.-b).

[KEY] An interval measures uncertainty from a specified procedure, conditional on its assumptions; it is not a cure for missing or wrongly measured pickups.

Failure mode: Reporting “42 ± 2.38 minutes” without identifying the parameter, confidence level, dates, or nonresponse limitation makes the number look more general than it is.

Try it — ungraded. For a separate illustrative mean of 30 minutes with SE 2 minutes and a supplied 95% critical value of 2, find the interval.

Answer. The margin is 2(2)=42(2)=4 minutes, so 30±4=[26,34]30\pm4=[26,34] minutes. This is an interval for a population mean only if the procedure’s sampling assumptions hold.

sections.title: 5. Estimate a proportion and plan useful precision
5.1 Slow-pickup interval and sample-size plan
sections.html:
A proportion is a share of units with a defined attribute: Cedar Loop’s slow=1 means more than 50 minutes, so exactly 50 is not slow. The simple normal-approximation, or Wald, interval is p^±z∗SEp^\hat p\pm z^*SE_{\hat p}. For a two-sided 95% interval, z∗≈1.96z^*\approx1.96. It is a useful introductory calculation when observations are suitable and expected counts are not small; with sparse successes or failures, a more appropriate proportion procedure is needed. Cedar Loop has 24 slow and 76 not-slow responses, so neither observed count is sparse. Its unresolved response process remains the more serious limitation. (The Pennsylvania State University, n.d.-c).

Worked example. Section 3 found SEp^≈0.04271SE_{\hat p}\approx0.04271. Complete the calculation without rounding the SE prematurely:

M=1.960.24(0.76)100≈1.96(0.042708)≈0.08371;M=1.96\sqrt{\frac{0.24(0.76)}{100}} \approx1.96(0.042708) \approx0.08371;
0.24−0.08371=0.15629,0.24+0.08371=0.32371.0.24-0.08371=0.15629,\qquad 0.24+0.08371=0.32371.

The illustrative 95% interval is 15.6% to 32.4%, rounded to one decimal percentage point. The 20% managerial target lies inside it. Thus these responses and this interval do not isolate a population slow share above 20%; they also do not establish that the target is met. More fundamentally, the interval does not incorporate the possible nonresponse bias demonstrated in Section 2. A bounded recommendation is to audit the frame and follow up nonrespondents, then plan an evening-focused staffing pilot with a labor-cost guardrail. The snapshot alone cannot establish a staffing effect. (The Pennsylvania State University, n.d.-b, n.d.-c).

Excel 365 check. With audited binary values in C2:C101, check =COUNT(C2:C101) is 100, =SUM(C2:C101) is 24, and every value is 0 or 1. Compute =SUM(C2:C101)/COUNT(C2:C101) for p^\hat p. If E5 holds that share and E2 holds 100, compute =SQRT(E5*(1-E5)/E2) for SE; subtract and add 1.96 times that cell for endpoints. For a summary-only check, enter =24/100 in E5. Excel verifies the arithmetic, not the selection mechanism. Microsoft documents the Excel statistical-function reference used for related checks. (Microsoft, n.d.).

For advance sample-size planning, specify an acceptable half-width MM before collection. For an approximate 95% one-proportion interval, with planning share p~\tilde p,

nusable≈(1.96M)2p~(1−p~).n_{\text{usable}}\approx \left(\frac{1.96}{M}\right)^2\tilde p(1-\tilde p).

If Cedar Loop wants roughly ±5 percentage points and uses the current respondent estimate p~=0.24\tilde p=0.24 as a planning input, then

nusable≈(1.96/0.05)2(0.24)(0.76)=280.283136,n_{\text{usable}}\approx (1.96/0.05)^2(0.24)(0.76) =280.283136,

so round up to 281 usable pickups. This is an approximate planning calculation, not a guarantee of exactly five points in the eventual interval. If no credible planning share exists, using p~=0.50\tilde p=0.50 gives the largest value of p~(1−p~)\tilde p(1-\tilde p): 1.962(0.25)/0.052=384.161.96^2(0.25)/0.05^2=384.16, rounded up to 385 usable pickups. At an assumed 80% usable-response rate, obtaining 281 usable pickups requires planning about 281/0.80=351.25281/0.80=351.25, or 352 invitations after rounding up. Inviting more people addresses count, not differential response. Sample-size plans for a mean instead require a planning standard deviation in minutes and a target margin in minutes. (The Pennsylvania State University, n.d.-c).

Failure mode: Reporting “±5%” when the intended margin is five percentage points, or treating 352 invitations as equivalent to 352 usable, representative observations.

Try it — ungraded. With the same planning share and confidence level, what happens to the approximate required usable sample size if the desired margin falls from 0.05 to 0.025?

Answer. The margin is halved and nn depends on 1/M21/M^2, so the unrounded requirement becomes four times as large: 4(280.283136)=1121.1325444(280.283136)=1121.132544. Round up to 1,122 usable pickups. This is a precision plan, not a nonresponse fix.

sections.title: 5.2 Optional bridge: differences between periods
sections.html:
A difference needs a defined order and unit. If Cedar Loop’s 100 respondents included 50 morning pickups with 10 slow and 50 evening pickups with 14 slow, those counts would agree with the case’s total of 24. The observed evening minus morning difference would be 14/50−10/50=0.28−0.20=0.0814/50-10/50=0.28-0.20=0.08, or 8 percentage points. For independent groups, the illustrative SE of that difference is

0.28(0.72)50+0.20(0.80)50=0.007232≈0.08504.\sqrt{\frac{0.28(0.72)}{50}+\frac{0.20(0.80)}{50}} =\sqrt{0.007232}\approx0.08504.

An introductory 95% normal interval is 0.08±1.96(0.08504)0.08\pm1.96(0.08504), or approximately −8.7 to 24.7 percentage points. With only 10 morning slow pickups, check whether a normal approximation is suitable before relying on it. The interval includes zero; neither its width nor an observed group difference makes time of day a causal explanation. Comparing mean minutes instead would estimate an evening-minus-morning mean in minutes, using both groups’ standard deviations and sample sizes. These are bridges to later comparison and testing sessions, not a staffing-effect analysis. (The Pennsylvania State University, n.d.-d).

Failure mode: Applying a one-proportion SE to a difference of two independent proportions, or describing an observational difference as the effect of adding staff.

Try it — ungraded. If two independent period estimates were 0.30 and 0.22, what is first minus second, and is that alone a causal result?

Answer. 0.30−0.22=0.080.30-0.22=0.08, or 8 percentage points. It is an observed contrast. Without a suitable design and uncertainty assessment, it is neither a demonstrated population difference nor a causal effect.

sections.title: 5.3 Optional bridge: interval for a difference between mean minutes
sections.html:
The previous bridge compared proportions of slow pickups in percentage points. A different question compares mean pickup durations in minutes. Suppose the same 100 responding pickups split into 50 morning and 50 evening responses. The morning mean is 40 minutes with sample standard deviation 11 minutes; the evening mean is 44 minutes with sample standard deviation 13 minutes. These fictional group summaries are compatible with the case's rounded overall mean of 42 minutes and standard deviation of about 12 minutes.

Worked example. Define the comparison direction before calculating: evening minus morning. The observed difference is 44−40=444-40=4 minutes. For two independent groups, Welch's estimated standard error uses each group's variance separately:

SExˉE−xˉM=13250+11250=5.8≈2.408 minutes.SE_{\bar x_E-\bar x_M} =\sqrt{\frac{13^2}{50}+\frac{11^2}{50}} =\sqrt{5.8}\approx2.408\text{ minutes}.

Welch's degrees of freedom are about 95 here, so the two-sided 95% critical value is about 1.985. The margin is 1.985(2.408)≈4.781.985(2.408)\approx4.78 minutes. The interval for the evening-minus-morning population mean difference is therefore about 4±4.784\pm4.78, or −0.78 to 8.78 minutes. It includes zero: these responses do not distinguish a positive population difference from zero at this interval's nominal level, even if sampling and response assumptions were satisfied. The unresolved nonresponse also limits that interpretation. Compare the groups' distributions and check for influential duration errors before reporting the interval. The comparison is observational; staffing was not varied, so it cannot estimate a staffing effect (The Pennsylvania State University, n.d.-d).

Excel 365 route. With audited morning minutes in one range and evening minutes in another, obtain each COUNT, AVERAGE, and STDEV.S; calculate =SQRT(s_evening^2/n_evening+s_morning^2/n_morning) from those summaries. Use a verified two-sided Welch critical value and record its degrees of freedom. SPSS route. An independent-samples t-test output can show an unequal-variances row and a confidence interval, but first confirm group coding, valid counts, and direction; do not copy the equal-variances row by habit (IBM, n.d.-c). The hand-calculated 2.4082.408 SE and approximately [−0.78,8.78][-0.78,8.78] interval are independent checks. Full test selection and effect interpretation belong to S08.

Try it — ungraded. If a colleague reports “morning minus evening = +4 minutes” from these summaries, what is wrong, and what happens to the interval when the subtraction order is reversed?

Answer. Morning minus evening is 40−44=−440-44=-4 minutes. Reversing the direction changes the signs of both interval endpoints, yielding approximately −8.78 to 0.78 minutes. It does not change the underlying evidence or remove the nonresponse limitation.

sections.title: Recap
sections.html:
• Name the population, period, unit, KPI, target, and decision before estimating anything.
  • Audit the sampling frame and preserve one record per eligible pickup.
  • Random selection of invitations does not guarantee representative responses.
  • Standard deviation describes unit-to-unit spread; standard error describes estimate-to-estimate spread.
  • A 95% interval is a repeated-procedure statement, conditional on its assumptions.
  • Calculate and report a mean interval in minutes; report a proportion interval in percentage points.
  • More usable independent observations usually improve random precision, but do not erase bias.
  • Choose sample size from a desired margin and a defensible planning value; round up.
  • Cedar Loop’s respondent evidence does not establish that the population exceeds its target or that staffing would change it.
  • Check arithmetic in Excel and, when authorized rows exist, SPSS; check provenance and missingness separately.

sections.title: Glossary
sections.html:
TermPlain-language meaning
PopulationEvery eligible unit covered by the stated question, such as the period’s 2,400 pickups.
UnitOne thing counted or measured; here, one completed pickup.
Sampling frameThe actual list of eligible units available for selection.
Simple random sampleA selection in which every same-sized set of distinct frame units has the same chance.
Stratified sampleRandom samples drawn separately within specified, nonoverlapping groups such as morning and evening pickups.
Cluster sampleRandomly selected groups of units, such as pickup waves, with several units observed within each group.
Systematic sampleSelection at a fixed interval on a list after a random start; list cycles can matter.
ParameterA fixed population quantity of interest, such as the true slow-pickup share.
StatisticA quantity calculated from a sample, such as 24 slow pickups out of 100 responses.
Point estimateOne sample statistic used to estimate a parameter.
BiasA systematic tendency for the data process to favor some results.
NonresponseA selected unit’s outcome being unavailable for the analysis.
IndependenceObservations supplying sufficiently separate information for the stated method.
Standard deviationA measure of spread among observed values, in the variable’s units.
Sampling distributionThe pattern a statistic would show across repeated samples of the same design.
Standard errorA measure of the spread of that sampling distribution.
Confidence intervalAn estimate range produced by a procedure with a stated long-run coverage level.
Welch intervalA two-independent-means interval that estimates each group's variance separately.
Margin of errorHalf an interval’s width when the interval is centered on its estimate.
PrecisionHow narrowly an estimate is reported under its stated procedure; it is not the same as freedom from bias.
